Every clinical trial submits its analyses as SAS programs: datasets, tables, listings and figures. The industry is moving to R, and each program has to be translated, and then proven to give the same result as the SAS original. Done by hand, that is weeks per study, and the proof is the expensive part.

sas2r-agent does both. It translates each program with a Meta model, and it proves equivalence by running the R and comparing every output against the SAS reference. This is the leaderboard of that proof, over one hundred programs.

One loop, four roles. The context builder reads the SAS program, its inputs, and the SAS outputs we are trying to match. The translator, Muse Spark 1.3 through the Meta Model API, writes one R script. A Docker sandbox with no network runs it. The comparator checks every output against the frozen SAS reference and sends the differences back as a repair prompt. Up to three attempts.

Here it is on two programs. The first matches on the first attempt. The second did not: the comparator reported which numbers were missing, sent them back as a repair prompt, and the second attempt matched.

Every attempt leaves a provenance record: hashes of the prompt, the answer, the script, every file produced, and the SAS reference it was compared with, chained into an append-only ledger. Verify recomputes the whole chain.

The benchmark is one hundred public SAS programs, ninety clinical and ten general, run in real SAS to produce the reference outputs. Claude Opus 5.5 is the baseline at ninety-seven percent. Muse Spark 1.3 reaches ninety-five, at half the price per correct translation.

This column is the one that matters for a company: the cost of one translation that fully matched SAS. Muse Spark is about ten cents. The open-weight Muse Spark Open runs at eighty-five percent on Baseten, so the whole pipeline also works without any API.

The agent improved from its own failures. Here is a listing the first prompt missed: only four of the three hundred and twelve SAS numbers appeared in the R output, and the comparison shows exactly that.

The failure analysis of those misses became prompt version two: eighty-six to ninety-five percent. The five remaining misses became version three, with the exact SAS formulas. Each version is its own row, so the improvement is measured on the same hundred programs, not claimed.
Any cell opens the generated R, the comparison report, and the provenance record with its position in the ledger.
